results.topic: How a vaccine trains the immune system

deck.title: How a vaccine trains the immune system
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: A vaccine introduces harmless pieces of a virus or bacteria into the body.
items.why: This safely exposes your immune cells to the invader without causing any actual disease or illness.
items.scene: A tiny, friendly cardboard cutout of a virus sits politely on a microscopic velvet chair.

check.wrong: Vaccines inject a mild, weakened form of the live disease that can sometimes still cause you to get sick.
check.right: Vaccines contain only harmless fragments or blueprints of the pathogen, never the live infectious disease.

items.link: Triggers the specialized white blood cells to investigate

items.answer: Specialized immune cells called macrophages spot the foreign fragments and sound the alarm.
items.why: Detection is vital because the body must recognize that these specific molecules do not belong there.
items.scene: A glowing security guard with a magnifying glass shines a bright spotlight on the cardboard virus.

check.wrong: White blood cells immediately destroy all foreign molecules floating in the blood without needing to inspect them first.
check.right: Specialized immune cells must first inspect and identify specific foreign molecules before mounting a targeted response.

items.link: Prompts the production of custom chemical weapons

items.answer: B cells build custom Y-shaped proteins called antibodies designed to latch onto the invader.
items.why: Antibodies must be custom-shaped to fit the specific invader like a key fitting precisely into a lock.
items.scene: A busy little workshop where tiny smiths hammer out millions of shiny, golden Y-shaped metal keys.

check.wrong: The body uses the exact same generic antibodies to fight off every different type of virus or bacteria.
check.right: The body manufactures unique, custom-shaped antibodies tailored specifically to fit the exact invader.

items.link: Leaves behind trained memory cells for the future

items.answer: Long-lived memory cells remain in the bloodstream to remember the invader for years.
items.why: These veteran cells ensure your body can respond instantly if the real pathogen ever tries to attack.
items.scene: An old, wise owl wearing a detective hat sits guard at the gateway, holding a wanted poster.

check.wrong: Once the vaccine fragments are cleared away, the immune system forgets the lesson and returns to its original state.
check.right: Long-lived memory cells persist in the body for years to provide rapid defense against future infections.

results.topic: How photosynthesis turns sunlight into sugar

deck.title: How photosynthesis turns sunlight into sugar
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Green pigment molecules inside chloroplasts absorb incoming photons from sunlight.
items.why: This absorption strips electrons away from water molecules, providing the raw electrical power needed to drive the entire reaction.
items.scene: A microscopic solar panel glowing bright emerald as tiny bright yellow light bullets crash into it.

check.wrong: Plants use sunlight directly to bake carbon dioxide and water into sugar like an oven.
check.right: Sunlight is only used to generate temporary power carriers, not to bake sugar directly.

items.link: Energized electrons travel down a protein chain.

items.answer: Enzymes break water molecules apart into oxygen gas, protons, and free electrons.
items.why: Splitting water is the only way to continuously replenish the electrons that the chlorophyll lost to the sunlight.
items.scene: A miniature pair of silver scissors slicing dripping water droplets into tiny floating gas bubbles.

check.wrong: Plants absorb water simply to keep their leaves cool and hydrated on hot days.
check.right: Plants chemically crack water apart to harvest its essential electrons for energy production.

items.link: Protons and electrons build a battery charge.

items.answer: Flowing protons snap chemical tags onto molecules to create rechargeable energy packets called ATP.
items.why: ATP acts as universal cellular currency, storing raw solar energy in chemical bonds for later use.
items.scene: Tiny glowing battery packs clicking into microscopic charging slots along a factory wall.

check.wrong: Plants store sunlight overnight inside glowing pockets of liquid light inside their stems.
check.right: Sunlight energy is converted into chemical bonds within rechargeable molecules like ATP.

items.link: Charged batteries power the next chemical cycle.

items.answer: Microscopic pores on the leaf underside suck in invisible carbon dioxide gas from the air.
items.why: Carbon dioxide supplies the essential carbon atoms needed to build the backbone of physical sugar molecules.
items.scene: A tiny open trapdoor on a giant leaf swallowing swirling grey clouds of gas.

check.wrong: Plants pull all their structural growth material up exclusively through their roots from the soil.
check.right: Most of a plant's solid mass comes from invisible carbon dioxide gas captured from the air.

items.link: Carbon atoms stitch together into sweet syrup.

items.answer: The plant uses stored ATP energy to stitch captured carbon atoms into glucose sugar.
items.why: Glucose provides stable, long-term chemical storage that the plant can eat for fuel or use to build wood.
items.scene: A bustling assembly line weaving glowing carbon beads into sticky white sugar cubes.

check.wrong: Sunlight fuses directly with carbon dioxide in a single instant flash to create sugar.
check.right: A complex cycle uses stored battery energy to painstakingly stitch carbon atoms together step by step.

check.wrong: The Earth's crust floats on a deep underground ocean of liquid water.
check.right: The crust floats on slowly churning, semi-solid rock mantle.

check.right: Fold mountains are formed by solid rock buckling under horizontal pressure without volcanoes.

check.wrong: Mountains will grow taller forever and eventually reach out into outer space.
check.right: Mountains reach a maximum height where the weight causes them to erode as fast as they rise.

items.scene: A regal official stands buried up to his neck in a swirling avalanche of flying white papers.

results.topic: What caused the 1929 stock market crash

deck.title: What caused the 1929 stock market crash
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Investors borrowed heavily to buy stocks, pushing prices far above their actual business value.
items.why: Easy credit created a false sense of endless wealth, encouraging risky financial bets across the country.
items.scene: A towering mountain of glittering gold coins resting precariously on a giant balloon that is slowly inflating.

check.wrong: The crash happened because the government suddenly outlawed all private stock trading overnight.
check.right: The crash happened because falling stock values triggered panic selling and unpaid borrowed loans.

items.link: Sparks a wave of sudden panic

items.answer: Fear spread rapidly as stock prices dipped, causing millions to try to sell at the exact same time.
items.why: When confidence evaporates, everyone rushes for the exit simultaneously, overwhelming the market's capacity to absorb trades.
items.scene: A massive stampede of paper stock certificates running frantically through a crowded banking hall.

check.wrong: Trading floors closed permanently because computers suffered a massive global power failure.
check.right: Trading floors were simply overwhelmed by the sheer volume of frantic human sellers.

items.link: Drives stock values downward instantly

items.answer: Stock values plummeted to near zero, wiping out fortunes accumulated over many years in hours.
items.why: With vastly more sellers than buyers, prices dropped violently until trading came to a near standstill.
items.scene: A towering glass skyscraper shattering completely into sparkling dust as a tiny feather touches it.

check.wrong: Every single company in the world went bankrupt and completely ceased operations forever.
check.right: Share prices collapsed even though many underlying businesses remained open and operational.

items.link: Triggers massive bank withdrawals

items.answer: Terrified citizens rushed to withdraw their savings, but banks had already lost money invested in the market.
items.why: Banks lent depositors cash to buy stocks, so when the market failed, the banks could not pay back customers.
items.scene: A desperate queue of people holding empty piggy banks outside a locked, heavy iron vault door.

check.wrong: Banks voluntarily closed their doors to give all their employees a long weekend holiday.
check.right: Banks closed because they ran out of physical cash after frightened customers emptied their vaults.

items.link: Plunges the economy into depression

items.answer: The financial collapse froze credit and spending, plunging the global economy into a decade of hardship.
items.why: Without functioning banks or consumer spending, businesses closed and millions lost their jobs and homes.
items.scene: A giant factory with its smokestacks completely cold, while a lone tumbleweed rolls across the empty entrance.

check.wrong: The economy recovered by the following Tuesday afternoon through normal market corrections.
check.right: The economic downturn lasted for a decade, requiring massive structural reforms to fix.

results.topic: How compound interest grows savings over time

deck.title: How compound interest grows savings

items.answer: Money placed in a savings account earns extra money called interest based on the principal amount.
items.why: Banks pay you to use your deposited money for their own lending activities.
items.scene: A shiny golden coin sitting in a glass jar suddenly splits into the original coin plus a smaller silver coin.

check.wrong: Interest is a flat fee paid by the bank once per year as a holiday bonus.
check.right: Interest is calculated continuously or periodically as a percentage of your total current balance.

items.link: adds this new money to the total

items.answer: The newly earned interest joins your original deposit to form a larger total balance.
items.why: Your account balance grows so that future calculations use a bigger starting figure.
items.scene: A tiny silver coin melts into the original golden coin, making the single coin visibly larger and heavier.

check.wrong: Earned interest is automatically separated and stored in a different untouchable account.
check.right: Earned interest merges directly into your main balance, increasing the amount eligible for future gains.

items.link: multiplies the next percentage cycle

items.answer: The next interest payment is calculated using the new, larger total rather than just the original deposit.
items.why: Percentage growth naturally yields bigger returns when applied to a larger overall sum.
items.scene: A larger golden coin splits into the big coin plus two silver coins instead of just one.

check.wrong: Interest is always calculated strictly against the original starting amount forever.
check.right: Compound interest calculates earnings on both the original principal and all accumulated past interest.

items.link: accelerates the growth speed over time

items.answer: The cycle repeats continuously, causing the total savings to grow faster and faster over long periods.
items.why: Exponential growth curves turn small early gains into massive totals if given enough time.
items.scene: A small rolling snowball rapidly transforms into a massive glowing boulder crashing across the room.

check.wrong: Compound interest grows steadily at the exact same straight-line speed every single year.
check.right: Compound interest accelerates exponentially, meaning the growth gets significantly faster with each passing year.

results.topic: How an index fund works

deck.title: How an index fund works

items.answer: Thousands of everyday investors combine their cash into one giant financial pool.
items.why: Pooling money gives everyday buyers the massive purchasing power usually reserved for wealthy investors and huge institutions.
items.scene: A giant glowing swimming pool filled with sparkling gold coins instead of water, with thousands of tiny hands pouring buckets in.

check.wrong: An index fund is a special private bank account managed entirely by a single wealthy stockbroker.
check.right: An index fund is a pooled collection of money owned collectively by thousands of ordinary individual investors.

items.link: buying a whole market index

items.answer: The fund manager uses the pooled cash to buy every company inside a specific stock market index.

items.scene: A giant robotic grocery shopper sweeping every single item off every supermarket shelf into one enormous shopping cart.

check.wrong: The fund manager constantly trades stocks every single day to chase quick profits and beat the market.
check.right: The fund manager simply buys and holds a fixed basket of stocks to match the overall market performance.

items.link: tracking steady market growth

items.answer: As the overall economy grows and companies make profits, the value of the fund rises steadily.

items.scene: A massive hot air balloon slowly rising into a clear blue sky, steadied by hundreds of strong ropes tied below.

results.topic: How a UPI payment moves money between two bank accounts

items.answer: The payer scans the receiver code using a smartphone payment app.

items.scene: A glowing smartphone shoots a laser beam at a pixelated square, freezing time in the room.

check.wrong: Scanning the code transfers money directly from your phone wallet to their phone.
check.right: Scanning the code only reads the receiver payment details to start the secure bank request.

items.answer: The payer types a confidential personal identification number to authorize the transfer.

items.scene: A giant digital keypad floats in mid-air, clicking shut like a heavy bank vault door.

check.wrong: Typing your PIN tells the merchant your secret banking password.
check.right: Your PIN safely unlocks your bank app to sign a one-time payment instruction.

items.link: Routes the signed instruction through the central server

items.answer: A unified payment network instantly relays the transaction request between different banks.
items.why: It acts as a universal translator so that any bank can talk to any other bank securely.
items.scene: A tiny digital train zooms through a glowing glass tube, switching tracks at high speed.

check.wrong: The payment network stores all your personal bank savings on its own private servers.
check.right: The payment network only routes messages and never holds your actual bank balance.

items.scene: An empty glass cup suddenly fills to the brim with sparkling golden liquid.

check.right: Oral or digital agreements are fully binding as long as offer, acceptance, and consideration exist.

results.topic: How HTTPS keeps a connection private

results.topic: How Git records and merges changes

items.why: This parent-child relationship guarantees that history cannot be altered without breaking all subsequent records.
items.scene: An old oak tree grows backwards in fast-motion, with each new branch firmly gripping the one below it.

check.wrong: Commits float independently in a random pile until you sort them manually by date.
check.right: Each commit permanently links to its parent commit, forming an unbroken chronological chain of history.

items.link: leads to branching for new features

items.answer: Branches are lightweight movable pointers that let you develop new features without risking working code.
items.why: Isolating experimental work prevents bugs from breaking the main software until they are fully ready.
items.scene: A train track splits mechanically into two separate glowing paths floating over a bottomless canyon.

check.wrong: Creating a branch duplicates your entire project folder on your computer's hard drive.
check.right: Branches are simply lightweight movable pointers pointing to a specific commit in the project history.

items.link: leads to merging different paths

items.answer: Git combines separate branches by finding their common ancestor and automatically integrating the new changes.
items.why: Automatic integration saves developers from manually copying and pasting code updates between different versions.
items.scene: Two glowing rivers flow toward each other and seamlessly blend into a single wider stream.

check.wrong: Merging automatically deletes all older versions of your code so they can never be recovered.
check.right: Merging combines separate branches by integrating their changes while preserving the full commit history.

items.link: leads to resolving conflicts

items.answer: When the same code line changes in both branches, Git pauses and asks you to choose the final version.
items.why: Computers cannot guess human intent, so developers must manually decide which conflicting change to keep.
items.scene: Two construction workers argue over a single doorway while holding opposite blueprints in a maze.

check.wrong: Git randomly deletes one of the conflicting changes without telling you when a merge clash occurs.
check.right: Git pauses the merge and asks a human developer to manually choose which conflicting version to keep.

results.topic: How a refrigerator keeps food cold

deck.title: How a refrigerator keeps food cold
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: A motorized pump increases the pressure of a special cooling fluid, making it hot.
items.why: Compressing a gas forces its molecules closer together, which rapidly concentrates heat energy and raises its temperature.
items.scene: A tiny mechanical fist tightly squeezing a glowing silver tube until it steams with heat.

check.wrong: The compressor creates cold air from nothing to chill the inside of the fridge.
check.right: The compressor only squeezes the refrigerant to increase its pressure and temperature.

items.link: flows into the condenser coils outside

items.answer: The hot fluid flows through black metal grids behind the fridge, dumping its heat into the room.
items.why: Heat naturally flows from a warmer area to a cooler room, allowing the fluid to cool down and turn into a liquid.
items.scene: A giant radiator sweating visible waves of shimmering orange heat into a cool bedroom.

check.wrong: The coils behind the fridge are designed to capture heat and trap it inside the walls.
check.right: The coils release the absorbed heat out into the surrounding room air.

items.link: rushes through the expansion valve

items.answer: The liquid passes through a tiny pinhole, causing its pressure to drop instantly and turning it freezing cold.
items.why: When a pressurized liquid suddenly expands into a wider space, it absorbs a massive amount of energy to change state.

items.answer: The freezing fluid travels through tubes inside the fridge, absorbing heat from your food and air.
items.why: Heat from inside the refrigerator moves into the freezing cold coils, leaving the interior chilled.
items.scene: A glowing red apple handing its warmth to a freezing blue snake wrapped around it.

check.wrong: Cold air is pumped in from an icebox hidden at the very bottom.
check.right: The cold coils absorb heat from the interior air, leaving the space chilled.

results.topic: How a flush toilet works

deck.title: How a flush toilet works
deck.subtitle: 6 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Pushing the flush handle lifts a connected chain attached to a rubber flapper valve at the bottom of the tank.
items.why: Lifting this valve opens the main escape route, allowing water to rush downward quickly using gravity.
items.scene: A tiny knight pulls a lever, yanking open a massive trapdoor at the bottom of a glass water tower.

check.wrong: The handle directly pushes the water out of the tank with mechanical force.
check.right: The handle only opens a valve, letting gravity pull the water down.

items.link: Water rushes rapidly down into the bowl below.

items.answer: Stored tank water surges through hidden rim holes and a siphon jet, quickly filling the porcelain bowl.
items.why: This sudden, large volume of water overwhelms the trap, creating the necessary conditions to trigger a siphon.
items.scene: A hundred tiny firehoses suddenly blast water around the inside rim of a giant white bowl.

check.wrong: Water slowly trickles in to push the waste out by weight alone.
check.right: Water surges in rapidly to fill the bowl and activate the siphon effect.

items.link: Rising water creates a powerful suction in the hidden trap.

items.answer: An S-shaped pipe creates a siphon, sucking all the water and waste out of the bowl into the drain.
items.why: The downward curve of the pipe removes air, and gravity pulls the liquid column down, creating suction.
items.scene: An energetic blue elephant uses its trunk to drink the entire contents of the bowl in one gulp.

check.wrong: Waste is pushed down the drain entirely by the sheer water pressure from above.
check.right: Waste is sucked down because the curved drain pipe creates a vacuum siphon.

items.link: An empty tank and empty bowl trigger the refill mechanism.

items.answer: As the water level inside the tank falls, a hollow plastic float drops down with the surface.
items.why: This floating ball acts as a sensor, tracking the water level to know when the tank needs refilling.
items.scene: A bright yellow rubber duck rides an elevator downward as the water level rapidly shrinks.

check.wrong: The float stays at the top until a timer tells the tank to start filling.
check.right: The float physically drops as the water level falls, triggering the fill valve.

items.link: A dropping float opens the fill valve to let new water in.

items.answer: The dropped float opens a fill valve, letting fresh water rush into the tank and refill it.
items.why: This restores the water supply so the toilet is ready for the next flush.
items.scene: A garden hose blasts fresh sparkling water back into the glass tank while a valve hisses loudly.

check.wrong: Fresh water fills the bowl directly instead of going into the tank first.
check.right: Fresh water fills the tank first to store energy for the next flush.

items.link: Rising water lifts the float back to its original position.

items.answer: As the water rises, the float rises with it until it shuts the fill valve completely.
items.why: This stops the water flow automatically, preventing the tank from overflowing onto the bathroom floor.
items.scene: A sleepy guard rises on a platform and slams a heavy vault door shut just in time.

check.wrong: You have to manually turn off the water supply after every single flush.
check.right: The rising float automatically shuts off the valve when the water reaches the right level.

results.topic: How noise-cancelling headphones work

deck.title: How noise-cancelling headphones work
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: A tiny microphone on the outside of the ear cup listens to environmental noise in real time.
items.why: The system must intercept sound waves before they reach your eardrum so it has time to process them.
items.scene: A tiny golden ear pressed against the outside of the headphone shell, straining to listen to the rushing traffic outside.

check.wrong: The microphone blocks the sound waves from physically entering the headphone cushion.
check.right: The microphone only records the sound waves to let the internal computer analyze them.

items.link: Sends the recorded sound wave into the digital processor.

items.answer: A digital chip instantly flips the incoming sound wave upside down, creating an exact mirror image.
items.why: Inverted waves have peaks where the original has troughs, setting up the conditions for cancellation.
items.scene: A tiny acrobat doing a vertical flip on a tightrope, turning every right-side-up wave completely upside down.

check.wrong: The processor deletes the sound data entirely to keep it from reaching your ear.
check.right: The processor transforms the sound data by inverting its phase into a mirror image.

items.link: Feeds the inverted wave to the internal speaker driver.

items.answer: The headphone speaker plays this inverted wave, known as anti-noise, directly into your ear canal.
items.why: Playing the opposite wave primes the sound fields to collide and neutralize each other.
items.scene: A miniature brass trumpet inside the speaker cone blasts out silent, upside-down ripples of sound.

check.wrong: The speaker plays louder music to drown out the annoying outside sounds.
check.right: The speaker plays a precise anti-noise wave designed specifically to combat the ambient hum.

items.link: Triggers destructive interference in the open air.

items.answer: The peak of the outside noise meets the trough of the anti-noise, causing them to cancel out.
items.why: When opposite wave values add together, they flatten to zero through destructive interference.
items.scene: Two ocean waves crashing into each other head-on and instantly flattening the water into a sheet of glass.

check.wrong: The two opposing sounds combine to create a much louder, combined mega-wave.
check.right: The two opposing waves subtract from each other, effectively silencing the ambient drone.

results.topic:
Water cycle notes (Year 9 geography)
- sun heats oceans/lakes -> evaporation, water vapour rises
- plants lose water from leaves = transpiration
- vapour cools higher up -> condenses on dust -> clouds
- droplets join, get heavy -> precipitation (rain, snow, hail)
- runoff over ground into rivers, some soaks in = infiltration -> groundwater
- rivers + groundwater flow back to sea, cycle repeats

deck.title: How the Water Cycle Works
deck.subtitle: 5 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: The sun warms up oceans and lakes, turning liquid water into invisible water vapour that rises.
items.why: Heat gives water molecules enough energy to break free from the liquid and float into the air as a gas.
items.scene: A giant smiling sun uses a huge red straw to slurp invisible steam off a sizzling ocean.

check.wrong: Water evaporates because boiling bubbles push the steam up into the sky.
check.right: Water evaporates slowly at normal temperatures when invisible vapour molecules escape into the air.

items.link: hot vapour rises high into the colder sky

items.answer: Plants suck water from soil and push it out of their leaves as invisible vapour.
items.why: This process called transpiration acts like a giant natural pump, moving water from underground up into the sky.
items.scene: A dramatic green fern sweating tiny glowing sweatbands off every single leaf.

check.wrong: Plants sweat water just like humans do to cool down on a hot day.
check.right: Plants pull water through their roots and release vapour through leaf pores to move nutrients.

items.link: vapour meets cold air high above

items.answer: Rising water vapour cools down high in the atmosphere and sticks to tiny dust specks to form clouds.
items.why: Cooling slows the vapour molecules down, causing them to bunch back together into liquid droplets.
items.scene: A fluffy white cloud wearing tiny spectacles, diligently knitting itself out of stray steam wisps.

check.wrong: Clouds are solid cotton-candy objects floating high up in the atmosphere.
check.right: Clouds are actually huge collections of trillions of microscopic liquid water droplets and ice crystals.

items.link: droplets grow too heavy and fall

items.answer: Cloud droplets collide and stick together until they become too heavy, falling down as rain.
items.why: Gravity pulls the massive water clusters back to Earth because the rising air can no longer hold them up.
items.scene: A grumpy cloud squeezing a massive blue sponge, making a huge puddle splash down below.

check.wrong: Clouds squeeze their water out like wet towels when the wind blows hard.
check.right: Rain happens because tiny cloud droplets combine until gravity pulls the heavy drops down.

items.link: water flows across the ground into rivers

items.answer: Water flows downhill across the land and through underground rocks, eventually returning to the ocean.
items.why: Gravity pulls all surface runoff and hidden groundwater downward, completing the endless loop.
items.scene: A goofy river wearing tiny running shoes, sprinting rapidly down a steep green mountain.

check.wrong: Water sinks into the ground and stays trapped underground forever.
check.right: Underground water slowly flows through rocks and soil, eventually feeding rivers that lead back to the sea.

results.topic: Why is the sky blue?

deck.title: Why is the sky blue?
deck.subtitle: 4 linked stages, taught by the Palace Architect

items.answer: Sunlight looks white to us, but it is actually made of every color of the rainbow mixed together.
items.why: White light from the sun carries all the colors of the light spectrum travelling together in waves.
items.scene: A giant glowing sun squeezes a rainbow toothpaste tube across the whole sky.

check.wrong: Sunlight is purely white light and contains no other colors inside it.
check.right: Sunlight is actually a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow combined.

items.link: travels down to touch the air

items.answer: The sunbeams crash into tiny invisible gas particles floating all around our planet.
items.why: Earth is wrapped in a thick blanket of air made of gases like nitrogen and oxygen.
items.scene: Bouncing pinballs made of sunlight crash into millions of tiny floating soap bubbles.

check.wrong: Sunlight passes straight through the air without touching any gases or particles.
check.right: Sunlight constantly crashes into tiny gas particles floating everywhere in the air.

items.answer: Blue light travels in short, choppy waves that crash into gas and scatter in every direction.
items.why: Shorter light waves hit obstacles much easier than long waves, causing them to bounce wildly.

check.right: Blue light travels in short waves that scatter in every direction when hitting gas.

items.answer: Our eyes catch all this scattered blue light bouncing around above us, so the sky looks blue.
items.why: The scattered blue light spreads all across the sky dome before reaching our eyes.
items.scene: A happy child wearing giant blue sunglasses looks up and smiles at the glowing roof.

check.wrong: The sky looks blue because it reflects the color of the deep ocean water.
check.right: The sky looks blue because scattered blue sunlight reaches our eyes from everywhere.
